claim: Lucic et al. name computational/hyperparameter-search budget as the confound that drives apparent differences between GAN algorithms, showing that most models reach similar FID scores given enough tuning budget.
stance_target: N1 sub-claim (a): naming a single specific unreported implementation choice as individually decisive for a headline comparison
scope_conditions: Generative adversarial networks: MM GAN, NS GAN, WGAN, WGAN-GP, LS-GAN, DRAGAN, BEGAN, VAE
quoted_support: We find that most models can reach similar scores with enough hyperparameter optimization and random restarts. This suggests that improvements can arise from a higher computational budget and tuning more than fundamental algorithmic changes.

claim: Lucic et al. give and execute a controlled protocol (shared architecture, matched hyperparameter-search budget k, bootstrap-CI result distributions instead of best-of-N) and show the published 'best algorithm' ranking dissolves once budget is controlled and honestly reported.
stance_target: N1 sub-claims (b) and (c): a protocol removing a confound and a demonstrated ranking change under control
scope_conditions: GAN comparison, FID metric, multiple datasets
quoted_support: there is no algorithm which clearly dominates others. Secondly, for an interesting range of FIDs, a 'bad' model trained on a large budget can out perform a 'good' model trained on a small budget.

claim: Lucic et al. isolate exactly one confound (compute/hyperparameter budget), not a taxonomy of multiple distinct confounds, and never run a variance decomposition (ANOVA/eta^2) attributing effect size to each of several confounds individually and jointly.
stance_target: N1: the multi-confound taxonomy with eta^2 quantification is already owned by this paper
scope_conditions: Full paper structure and methodology section
quoted_support: Computational budget: Depending on the budget to optimize the parameters, different algorithms can achieve the best results. We explore how the results vary depending on the budget k, where k is the number of hyperparameter settings for a fixed model.
numbers: budget k = number of hyperparameter settings per model

claim: Lucic et al.'s single-axis confound (compute/hyperparameter budget) is the closest analogue among the four batch papers to N1's factor (iii) optimizer tuning, but does not touch surrogate-side confounds specific to offline MBO (target scaling, candidate/oracle protocol, ensemble size K, acquisition pessimism beta).
stance_target: residual specific to offline MBO not owned by this paper
scope_conditions: cross-domain comparison, GAN evaluation vs offline MBO surrogate/optimizer decomposition
quoted_support: instead of random search it might be beneficial to apply (carefully tuned) sequential Bayesian optimization which is computationally beyond the scope of this study

claim: Lucic et al. find no evidence that any tested GAN algorithm consistently outperforms the non-saturating GAN (NS-GAN) baseline once budget and variance are properly accounted for.
stance_target: N9-adjacent: reality-check papers typically find effects shrink or vanish under audit (the opposite direction from the offline MBO paper's claimed effect growth)
scope_conditions: GAN comparison across datasets and architectures
quoted_support: we did not find evidence that any of the tested algorithms consistently outperforms the non-saturating GAN introduced in [9].
